apush-saq-0059.a: The Awakening challenged established authority when itinerant preachers drew crowds away from settled ministers and told hearers to trust their own conversion experience over the minister's word.
apush-saq-0059.b: Revival preaching put the test of true religion inside the hearer: a conversion felt in the heart mattered more than a minister's learning or a church's approval, so colonists who judged a preacher by their own experience were practicing independent judgment.
apush-saq-0059.c: Historians disagree because the evidence pulls both ways: the revivals taught defiance of authority, yet the fires had died decades before 1776 and many patriot leaders were never awakened.

apush-saq-0060.a: German immigrants — the Germans Franklin feared would 'Germanize' Pennsylvania.
apush-saq-0060.b: Franklin feared the Germans would become so numerous that they would Germanize Pennsylvania instead of adopting English language and customs, so the colony would lose its English character.
apush-saq-0060.c: Pennsylvania's diversity shaped the colony by drawing settlers from across Europe — Welsh, German, and others settled in their own townships — and by making toleration and a representative assembly part of its government under the Charter of Privileges.

apush-saq-0061.a: An older woman in a shawl is led away along a snowy path by armed men carrying muskets, one of them holding a paper warrant — the arrest of an accused witch.
apush-saq-0061.b: The painting was made in 1883, nearly two centuries after the Salem trials of 1692, so it shows how 19th-century Americans imagined the trials, not what an arrest actually looked like in 1692.
apush-saq-0061.c: The Puritan belief in a cosmic struggle between God and Satan active in daily life made witchcraft plausible: sickness, bad harvests, and strange fits could be read as the devil's work.

apush-saq-0062.a: The power of the purse — the House refused to vote Governor Burnet a fixed salary of 1,700 pounds, paying him year by year instead.
apush-saq-0062.b: By controlling the governor's salary, the assembly could pressure him: a governor who depended on yearly votes for his pay had to listen to the representatives, since whoever controlled the purse controlled the government.
apush-saq-0062.c: Assemblies claiming the power of the purse, electing representatives, and making laws showed colonists governing themselves — as in the Mayflower Compact and the Fundamental Orders, colonists created their own governments by agreement.

apush-saq-0063.a: Locke claims the magistrate's power consists only in outward force — fines, prisons, and punishments — and so cannot reach souls.
apush-saq-0063.b: True religion consists in the inward persuasion of the mind, which no outward force can produce. A magistrate can compel outward conformity but cannot compel belief, so his power is the wrong tool for souls.
apush-saq-0063.c: Locke's argument shaped later 18th-century advocates of toleration, who used it to defend dissenters against established churches. The claim that government cannot compel belief became a foundation for religious freedom in America.

apush-saq-0064.a: New England was settled by families who came together for religion and built compact towns around a church and a common, while the Chesapeake was settled mostly by single young men, indentured servants, who scattered along the rivers on tobacco plantations.
apush-saq-0064.b: The Chesapeake developed scattered plantations because tobacco farming needed large tracts of riverfront land, worked by indentured servants who came as single laborers rather than families building towns.
apush-saq-0064.c: Both regions were settled by English migrants in the 1600s and developed under English law and government, with elected assemblies.

apush-saq-0065.a: The Act protects anyone in Maryland professing to believe in Jesus Christ from being troubled, molested, or discountenanced for their religion, guaranteeing the free exercise of their religion within the province.
apush-saq-0065.b: Maryland was founded by Lord Baltimore as a refuge for Catholics, and Catholics and Protestants lived side by side there. The Act was meant to keep the peace between them by promising no Christian would be punished for their faith.
apush-saq-0065.c: The Act protected only Christians: anyone who denied the Trinity or blasphemed God could be put to death under the same Act, and Jews and people of other faiths had no protection at all.

apush-saq-0066.a: Pilgrims kneel and stand in prayer on the deck of the ship Speedwell around an open Bible, with a rainbow behind them and a sail above reading 'God with us'; armor and a musket lie on the deck in the foreground.
apush-saq-0066.b: The painting reflects 19th-century Americans remembering the Pilgrims as pious, God-guided founders — a heroic religious founding story, fitting for a painting hung in the Capitol Rotunda.
apush-saq-0066.c: The painting was made in 1843, more than two centuries after the Pilgrims' departure, so it is a 19th-century imagining of the event, not a record of what the departure actually looked like.

apush-leq-0020.thesis: The Awakening and the Enlightenment both challenged established authority, but by opposite means: the Awakening through emotion and conversion, the Enlightenment through reason and experiment, and both taught colonists to judge authority for themselves.
apush-leq-0020.contextualization: Before the revivals, colonial churches were settled and formal, with declining conversions and shrinking membership; at the same time print culture and scientific thinking were spreading.
apush-leq-0020.evidence_1: Edwards's sermons on human depravity, Whitefield's itinerant preaching to crowds in the thousands, and the New Light-Old Light split.
apush-leq-0020.evidence_2: Franklin's experiments and his measurement of Whitefield's crowd, Locke's ideas on toleration, and Deist belief in a distant creator.
apush-leq-0020.comparison: The Awakening challenged authority through emotion and conversion felt in the heart, while the Enlightenment challenged it through reason and experiment.
apush-leq-0020.complexity: The two movements overlapped and sometimes reinforced each other, and both were resisted by established churches and ministers.

apush-leq-0021.thesis: Colonial self-government grew mainly from colonial initiative, with British neglect creating the room for it: neglect alone did not create assemblies, colonists claimed the powers themselves.
apush-leq-0021.contextualization: The colonies were founded under charters an ocean away from London, and assemblies had been growing since the 1600s.
apush-leq-0021.evidence_1: Lax enforcement of the Navigation Acts, salutary neglect under Walpole, and the long gaps between royal instructions.
apush-leq-0021.evidence_2: The Mayflower Compact, the Fundamental Orders, and assemblies claiming the power of the purse, as in Massachusetts refusing Governor Burnet a fixed salary in 1728.
apush-leq-0021.causation: Distance and lax enforcement left room that assemblies filled: when London did not govern closely, colonists governed themselves.
apush-leq-0021.complexity: Neglect and initiative worked together, and self-government grew unevenly across colonies and remained bounded by royal authority.

apush-leq-0022.thesis: By 1754 the colonies had developed strongly distinct regional identities — different economies, churches, and societies — but shared language, law, and assemblies kept them one British world.
apush-leq-0022.contextualization: The colonies were founded for different purposes, by different peoples, an ocean away from London.
apush-leq-0022.evidence_1: New England's compact towns and Puritan church, the Chesapeake's tobacco plantations, the Middle Colonies' diversity, and South Carolina's rice plantations.
apush-leq-0022.evidence_2: Shared English language and law, Protestant worship, trade with Britain, and elected assemblies.
apush-leq-0022.comparison: Distinct economies and churches made the regions different, while shared language, law, and assemblies tied them together.
apush-leq-0022.complexity: The same forces both divided and united the colonies, and identities varied within regions as well as between them.
